text: A supplied coupling has the required marginals, so its Lp displacement is one member of the family whose infimum defines Wp. The inequality has the correct direction, matching [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s transport-plan definition. No minimizer or finite-cost assumption is needed. The [two-Dirac calibration](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L487) passes, making this bound an equality for a nonzero exponent. At p=0 or ∞ it remains the same order-theoretic bound for Mathlib’s stated Lp convention.
Two-Dirac calibration: for nonzero p the actual distance equals ground edist; choosing equal atoms gives zero.

The graph plan of the a.e. measurable map T couples μ with T♯μ, and pushing the Lp objective back to μ gives exactly `edist x (T x)`. Thus the right side measures displacement of the same map, as in [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s admissible-plan bound. Joint measurability of the ground cost justifies that change of measure. The [translation upper-bound Check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Convolution.lean#L128) passes; the [canonical real-space equality](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Convolution.lean#L197) also passes for p≥1. The theorem itself does not require T to be Lipschitz.
Translation upper-bound Check: specialize the displacement estimate to x↦x+a for a probability law.
Canonical translation equality Check: on a real seminormed space and1≤p, Wp of a law and its translate is exactly enorm(a), without a moment assumption.

The hypothesis bounds every admissible coupling’s Lp displacement from below, so it bounds their infimum from below. This is the universal lower-bound property of [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s variational definition. The universal quantifier over couplings is essential: one expensive plan would not suffice. With no coupling the infimum is ∞ and the implication remains correct. The [two-Dirac identity](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L487) uses this lower-bound API to recover the exact ground distance, providing a native calibration.
Two-Dirac calibration: for nonzero p the actual distance equals ground edist; choosing equal atoms gives zero.

Strictly below a threshold means that some admissible plan already has objective below that threshold. This follows from the infimum in [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82) and the linear complete order on ENNReal. The strict inequalities are crucial; equality with the infimum would require an attainment result. The [finite-distance coupling consequence](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L259) passes by taking the threshold ∞. At threshold zero both sides are false, and with no couplings both sides are false for every threshold.
At threshold∞ the strict-infimum characterization produces a coupling; no attainment is asserted.

An infimum in [0,∞] is ∞ exactly when every member of the family is ∞. Lean quantifies over every measure and then its coupling proof, precisely the admissible plans in [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82). The empty family is correctly included: the [no-coupling theorem](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L253) passes. This criterion also covers existing couplings with infinite objective. It does not mistake one infinite-cost coupling for an infinite optimal value.
The empty admissible family gives infinite Wasserstein value.

A finite infimum yields a plan with objective below ∞, hence a coupling, exactly as the [strict-threshold criterion](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L219) states. The converse really fails: for δ₀ and Cauchy(0,1), [the unique-coupling formula](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L454) and [nonintegrability of the Cauchy identity](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/Probability/Distributions/Cauchy/Basic.lean#L249) give infinite W₁ despite existence of a coupling. Here “infinite value” must mean the optimal value in this unique-plan example; a single bad plan alone would not establish that. No optimal coupling is claimed.
A strict finite threshold has a genuine admissible witness below it.
The Dirac-source plan is unique and its cost is exactly the distance-section Lp seminorm.

At location0 and scale1, Cauchy identity is nonintegrable. Combined with the published distance/Lp¹ interfaces this gives the Dirac/Cauchy infinite-W1 example; this theorem alone is not labelled a standalone Wasserstein fixture.

The diagonal graph plan has both marginals μ and zero displacement almost everywhere, so its objective and the infimum are zero. This is the diagonal case of [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s distance construction. `[MeasurableEq X]` makes the diagonal argument valid even without globally measurable ground distance. The [two-Dirac calibration](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L487) passes and specializes to zero for equal atoms. The theorem covers zero or infinite measures and both endpoint exponents; no separation of points is used.
Two-Dirac calibration: for nonzero p the actual distance equals ground edist; choosing equal atoms gives zero.

Swapping coordinates sends a coupling of μ,ν to one of ν,μ and leaves its objective unchanged because ground edist is symmetric. This gives exactly Wp(μ,ν)=Wp(ν,μ), as in [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82). The explicit joint-measurability hypothesis supports the change-of-measure identity. The [right-Dirac formula](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L514) passes as a concrete consequence of symmetry and the left-Dirac formula. Infinite values and p=∞ cause no exception; probability normalization is unnecessary here.
The right-Dirac identity verifies the cost orientation after symmetry.

For p≤q, each admissible plan is a probability measure because its first marginal is. The probability-space Lp inequality therefore gives Wp≤Wq after taking infima, matching [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s Remark 6.5. Retaining the probability hypothesis avoids the mass-dependent scaling of general Lp norms. The [Dirac Check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L487) passes with equality for nonzero exponents. At p=0 Mathlib’s zero-exponent convention applies; at q=∞ the upper norm is the essential-supremum norm when measurable.
Two-Dirac calibration: for nonzero p the actual distance equals ground edist; choosing equal atoms gives zero.

A coupling with first marginal δx and probability second marginal ν is the pushforward of ν by y↦(x,y). Its Lp cost is therefore exactly the displayed norm of `edist x y`; this is the Dirac-component identity required by [Layer 3.2](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/4f7a4021c5eefb6a254dcd4db450663a5f1aa71d/TauCetiRoadmap/OptimalTransport/README.md#L510). The [two-Dirac calibration](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L487) passes, agreeing with [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s Example 6.2. Joint measurability justifies evaluating that plan. The identity includes p=∞ as an essential-supremum formula and p=0 with Mathlib’s convention.
Two-Dirac calibration: for nonzero p the actual distance equals ground edist; choosing equal atoms gives zero.

The [unique-coupling identity](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L454) turns Wp(δx,ν) into the Lp norm of distance from x. Joint measurability supplies the measurability part of `MemLp`, so finiteness of that norm is exactly the left side. This proves the specified-basepoint criterion in [Layer 3.2](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/4f7a4021c5eefb6a254dcd4db450663a5f1aa71d/TauCetiRoadmap/OptimalTransport/README.md#L510), including p=∞ as essential boundedness. The [Dirac calibration](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L487) passes. On an extended metric space this fixes x; it does not claim independence across infinitely separated components.
Two-Dirac calibration: for nonzero p the actual distance equals ground edist; choosing equal atoms gives zero.

Triangle inequalities bound either distance section by the other plus the finite constant d(x₀,x₁). On a finite measure, adding that constant preserves Lp membership. Both a.e. measurability hypotheses are explicit. This is [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s basepoint independence with exactly the extended-metric restriction required by [Layer 3.1](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/4f7a4021c5eefb6a254dcd4db450663a5f1aa71d/TauCetiRoadmap/OptimalTransport/README.md#L510). The [finite-Dirac-distance transfer](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L583) passes. The finite-distance hypothesis correctly prevents changing to a different extended-metric component, and the argument also covers p=∞.
Finite Wasserstein distance from a Dirac basepoint transfers along a finite ground distance, using the stated section measurability.

Gluing plans for μ–ν and ν–ρ gives a μ–ρ plan; the ground triangle inequality and Lp Minkowski bound its displacement. This is precisely [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s argument. The signature retains standard-Borel structure, measurable ground distance, finite middle measure, and p≥1. It does not assume optimal plans exist. The [two-Dirac Check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L487) reduces the assertion to the ground triangle inequality. The [pseudometric Dirac control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Quotient.lean#L87) also passes; separation is not claimed by this theorem.
Two-Dirac calibration: for nonzero p the actual distance equals ground edist; choosing equal atoms gives zero.
Pseudometric control: zero-distance atoms have zero Dirac Wasserstein distance. For the Borelσ-algebra those Dirac laws already agree; no claim of distinct laws is made.

On an ordinary pseudometric space, `edist x y = ENNReal.ofReal (dist y x)` and distance is nonnegative. The two functions therefore have identical extended norms, giving exactly the displayed `MemLp` equivalence. This matches [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s real-distance moment convention and [Mathlib’s norm-based definition](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Function/LpSeminorm/Defs.lean#L92). The supplied a.e. strong measurability of real distance transfers through `ofReal`. No finite-measure hypothesis is necessary for this pointwise conversion; p=0 and p=∞ are included.

`HasFiniteMoment p ν` supplies one basepoint with finite Lp distance. In an ordinary pseudometric space every other basepoint is at finite distance from it, so the [published basepoint comparison](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L563) gives the stated `MemLp` conclusion. This is [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s basepoint independence. The signature correctly keeps finite mass and a.e. strong measurability of the requested section. It includes p=∞ but does not extend the claim to arbitrary components of an extended metric space.
Basepoint transfer uses finite ground distance, finite measure, and both a.e. strong measurability conditions.

A real K-Lipschitz function obeys |f(y)|≤|f(x₀)|+K·d(y,x₀). Finite mass integrates the constant, and finite first moment integrates the distance, proving exactly `Integrable f ν`. Measurable opens make continuous f and distance measurable. This justifies the Lipschitz test functions used in [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s Kantorovich–Rubinstein formula. The [Cauchy identity theorem](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/Probability/Distributions/Cauchy/Basic.lean#L249) supplies a concrete guardrail: Cauchy(0,1) cannot satisfy this first-moment hypothesis when f is the identity.

At location0 and scale1, Cauchy identity is nonintegrable. Combined with the published distance/Lp¹ interfaces this gives the Dirac/Cauchy infinite-W1 example; this theorem alone is not labelled a standalone Wasserstein fixture.

The a.e. finite-set condition bounds distance from x₀ by the maximum of finitely many finite ground distances. Finite mass and that bound give `MemLp` for every exponent, exactly the finite-support case of [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s moment definition. The explicit x₀ supplies a basepoint even when the measure is zero. The [Dirac moment Check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L687) passes for the one-atom case. At p=∞ this proves essential boundedness; it makes no finite-support density claim for the W∞ topology.
The actual Dirac measure has finite p-moment for every exponent, including∞.

The existential condition “finite Lp distance from some point” is equivalent to the condition at the displayed x. The forward implication is the [basepoint-independence theorem](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L638); the reverse simply uses x as the witness. This is [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s assertion that Pp does not depend on its basepoint. Finite mass, ordinary pseudometric distance, and measurability of the chosen section are explicit. Thus the statement includes essential boundedness at p=∞ without making an unrestricted extended-component claim.
Existential moment membership transfers to each prescribed measurable distance section.

For 0<p<∞, finite Lp distance is equivalent to finiteness of ∫d(x,y)^p dν. Lean expresses these endpoint exclusions as `p≠0` and `p≠∞`, then uses `p.toReal` inside the power. The result matches [Villani, Chapter 6](https://www.ceremade.dauphine.fr/~mischler/articles/VBook-O%26N.pdf#page=82)’s Definition 6.3 and the [Lp convention](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Function/LpSeminorm/Defs.lean#L92). Ordinary pseudometric distance, measurable opens and finite mass justify the arbitrary basepoint. The [Dirac moment Check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L687) passes. The exclusions prevent incorrectly treating the infinity exponent as a zeroth-power integral.
The actual Dirac measure has finite p-moment for every exponent, including∞.

This combines basepoint independence with the [unique Dirac-coupling formula](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L454): a probability law has finite p-moment exactly when Wp from δx is finite. It is the Dirac-component identification prescribed by [Layer 3.2](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/blob/4f7a4021c5eefb6a254dcd4db450663a5f1aa71d/TauCetiRoadmap/OptimalTransport/README.md#L510). The [Dirac moment Check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L687) and [two-Dirac distance Check](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/d96e9ceca01f4548b817649c5ae95e33c6fc3ae4/TauCeti/MeasureTheory/OptimalTransport/Wasserstein/Basic.lean#L487) pass. Ordinary pseudometric distance permits replacing the existential basepoint by x. The equivalence includes p=∞ as essentially bounded distance and does not identify components of arbitrary infinite-moment anchors.
The actual Dirac measure has finite p-moment for every exponent, including∞.
Two-Dirac calibration: for nonzero p the actual distance equals ground edist; choosing equal atoms gives zero.
